video_title: Jack Mallers on Leaving 21: "Now I Can Tell You Whatever You Want"
gist: Jack Mallers, freshly resigned from Bitcoin treasury company 21 (co-founded with Tether, second-largest corporate BTC treasury at 43,514 BTC) and no longer bound by public-company disclosure rules, explains that he walked away from a ~3% stake worth hundreds of millions rather than fold Strike into 21 after investors pressured the board to consolidate. He argues 2025 was never a real bull market (Bitcoin never made new highs versus gold), that Bitcoin is a hybrid of disruptive technology plus expectations of future fiat liquidity, and that genuine Bitcoin understanding is closer to 800,000 people globally — a basis point — leaving room for a $10-20 trillion asset before 1% adoption.

themes.theme: Why 21 was built and why Mallers walked

insights.claim: Jack Mallers co-founded Bitcoin treasury company 21 with Tether — specifically chairman Giancarlo Devasini and CEO Paolo Ardoino — and says Tether constitutes the board, meaning he never controlled the company he named, ticker-registered and logo-designed.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Governance, not operations, was the binding constraint at 21 — investors in Tether-backed vehicles should assume Tether's board controls strategy regardless of who fronts the brand.
insights.quote: 21 was never mine. Um it was always up to the board. Uh Tether makes up the board and so at a certain point we began to disagree

insights.claim: Mallers frames the Bitcoin-equity landscape as a spectrum with Coinbase and Robinhood at one end (customers, cash flow, products, DCF-valuable but low Bitcoin conviction) and Strategy/Michael Sailor at the other (maximum Bitcoin conviction but self-described capital markets financial engineering with no products or cash flow), with 21 designed as the missing middle.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for screening crypto equities: score each name on conviction versus cash-flow durability, and treat 'middle' vehicles as unproven rather than automatically superior.
insights.quote: can we build a business that has products and cash flow and growth prospects whilst also displaying an immense amount of singular focus conviction in this Bitcoin thing?

insights.claim: Mallers reads Coinbase's balance sheet as roughly $10-11 billion of assets with less than $1 billion in Bitcoin, calling that under 10% conviction in Bitcoin expressed monetarily.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Balance-sheet composition is a cheap proxy for where a listed crypto operator's real incentives sit — useful when picking between Bitcoin-levered and altcoin-levered equity exposure.
insights.quote: if you look at their balance sheet, they've got 10 11 billion and less than one is Bitcoin

insights.claim: Mallers says the original founding agreement explicitly excluded folding Strike into 21, but investors later lobbied the board to have him consolidate the two because they could not tell which company his announcements and keynotes applied to.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Founder-brand overlap across a private company and a public vehicle is a live conflict risk that markets will eventually force to resolve — usually against the private company's independence.
insights.quote: the market wants Jack to consolidate like when Jack announces something or does a keynote is is he talking about the thing that I bought or like what's the difference

insights.claim: Mallers forfeited an approximately 3% ownership stake in 21 — which he estimates at hundreds of millions of dollars given a multibillion-dollar company valuation — rather than sell or merge Strike.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Quantifies the founder's revealed preference: Strike's independence was priced above nine figures, a signal about how he will resist future acquisition or public-listing pressure.
insights.quote: I was 3% owner of 21, which I no longer

insights.claim: Mallers describes the departure decision as a blank-check buyout offer that he rejected instinctively before reasoning it through, framing it as a test of stated principles rather than a strategic calculation.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Sets expectations that Strike will not be sold or taken public on financial terms alone — relevant to anyone modeling a Strike exit or secondary.
insights.quote: here's a blank check and here's what you anything you want. Like, are you willing to to sell out? And you know, it was interesting is before I could even like reason it out, I found myself like I just couldn't. There's just no way.

insights.claim: Mallers explicitly calls his 21 tenure a failure because he communicated a vision and set public expectations he could not meet, while insisting the company itself has not failed and retains the second-largest corporate treasury, NYSE listing and a capable board.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Separates founder-departure headline risk from underlying asset quality — 21 holders are being told the balance sheet is intact even as the founder narrative collapses.
insights.quote: I communicated a vision and I communicated expectations that weren't met and I I need to own that

insights.claim: Mallers says he is legally free to speak now that he is no longer a public company officer reporting to the SEC, and that being a public-company officer was excruciatingly painful and constrained how he could communicate with Bitcoiners.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Explains the information vacuum around treasury companies during drawdowns, and suggests more candid Strike-side disclosure going forward than 21 shareholders will get.
insights.quote: now that I'm not a public company officer, uh, reporting to the SEC, I could tell you whatever you want

insights.claim: Mallers declines to comment on 21's forward roadmap and says he expects the company itself to communicate its plan to shareholders soon, which is what he would do if still leading it.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Flags a near-term catalyst: a strategy update from 21 that will reprice the equity independent of Mallers' departure.

themes.theme: Treasury-company mechanics and the window that closed

insights.claim: 21 launched in April 2025 as the first treasury company of this era — ahead of Adam Back's Nakamoto — into a market Mallers describes as uncrowded, with liquidity and exuberance, conditions that no longer exist.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: First-mover timing in the treasury-company trade mattered less than execution speed; later entrants faced strictly worse financing conditions.
insights.quote: we were the first, we were before, I'm trying to think of the file, uh, Adam Bax one, uh, Nakamoto. Um, this was April 2025

insights.claim: The October US government shutdown froze SEC review and pushed 21's NYSE listing approval from the expected summer to December, so the company could not deploy raised cash or operate during the most favorable window.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Regulatory-calendar risk is a real, unhedgeable cost for pre-listing vehicles — a template for how shutdowns can destroy a capital-markets thesis.
insights.quote: like we're ready to run the business and well the government someone plugged the government back in. What do you mean it's not on? And uh they couldn't approve us. And so we didn't get approved until December.

insights.claim: Because 21 legally could not buy Bitcoin with its raised cash before SEC approval, Mallers asked Tether to front the purchase and buy the Bitcoin itself, with 21 repaying Tether post-approval — which he says explains, but does not validate, claims that the treasury was merely pledged by Tether.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Clarifies a contested balance-sheet point for 21 holders: the BTC was funded by real raised capital, with Tether acting as a bridge rather than a donor.
insights.quote: Well, why doesn't Tether front us by buying the Bitcoin themselves and then we'll pay Tether back once we get approved?

insights.claim: 21 raised a little under $1.5 billion, bought over $1 billion of Bitcoin, and holds 43,514 BTC visible in proof of reserves — which Mallers uses to reject accusations that the venture was a rug pull.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: A hard NAV floor for anyone valuing 21 equity against its mNAV: the coins are verifiable on chain.
insights.quote: it's not like the 43,514 Bitcoin aren't sitting in our proof of reserves. I mean, you could see them. So the money's there, the business is there, the equity's on the New York Stock Exchange.

insights.claim: Between 21's filing and its approval the financing regime for treasury companies inverted: the definition of mNAV shifted repeatedly, the premium available for selling equity at the market compressed, and convertible instruments gave way to preferred as the strategy of choice.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: The treasury-company playbook is regime-dependent — track ATM premium and the convert-versus-preferred mix as the leading indicator of whether these vehicles can still accrete BTC per share.
insights.quote: the definition of MNAV has changed 700 times. Um the premium to the equity of selling the ATM has changed. All of a sudden, you know, convertible instruments um were not the strategy and it was preferred

insights.claim: Mallers argues cash flow, not financial engineering, is the cheapest non-dilutive way to grow Bitcoin per share, and that this was the core bet behind 21 — that capital pools already buying perpetual preferred would prefer a Bitcoin-converted operating business.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: The sats-per-share metric favors profitable operators over pure leverage vehicles when equity premiums vanish — a screen for which treasury names survive the bear market.
insights.quote: what's the best thing for SATs per share is like cash flow. That's the best non-dilutive easiest way to do it.

insights.claim: Mallers and Tether waited for an incumbent like Robinhood to adopt a Bitcoin-conviction balance sheet for the network effects and economies of scale, and only built 21 when nobody did.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: The strategic gap he identified is still unfilled — an existing high-cash-flow fintech converting its treasury to Bitcoin remains an unexploited move.
insights.quote: I was really waiting for like Robin Hood or someone to say, "Man, displaying conviction in Bitcoin carries so much network effects, so many economies of scale."

insights.claim: Mallers rejects blanket criticism of Bitcoin treasury companies, framing Bitcoin as a public utility where any use consistent with consensus rules is legitimate, rather than a movement that can be betrayed by institutional adoption.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the retail narrative that treasury vehicles are inherently bad, arguing they should be judged individually on structure rather than dismissed as a category.
insights.quote: Bitcoin is a public ledger, public code, and you use it for what you want. As long as you're following the consensus rules, which are, you know, what governs the network and how the software works, then all is fair game.

insights.claim: Mallers says the public listing process required selecting a primary market maker — meetings included Citadel — and that Citadel's willingness to provide equity liquidity without knowing his balance sheet or understanding Bitcoin is precisely what capital-markets regulation is designed to enable.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Explains the structural trade a Bitcoin company makes when listing: regulatory compliance buys institutional liquidity provision that no libertarian workaround can replicate.
insights.quote: Citadel's basically going to plow like a ton of money into providing our equity liquidity so that we can raise capital so that our investors can get in and get out

themes.theme: Cycle read: 2025 was not a real bull market

insights.claim: Mallers does not count 2025 as a genuine bull run and says Bitcoin failed to make new all-time highs measured against gold, only in nominal dollar terms.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Argues the BTC/gold ratio, not the dollar price, is the correct cycle indicator — a chart to watch before declaring a new bull phase.
insights.quote: Bitcoin did not make new highs against gold. Um it did not make new highs. I mean, I I view looking at the world in fiat is like wearing drunk goggles.

insights.claim: Mallers attributes the absence of a real bull market to monetary policy that has been restrictive since 2021 — the fastest rate hiking cycle ever, rates held elevated because inflation proved stickier than expected, and a sharply shrunken Fed balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Frames the next real Bitcoin bull market as gated on a policy pivot rather than on adoption news flow.
insights.quote: monetary policy has been immensely restrictive since 2021. Uh rates have remained elevated because inflation has been stickier and more persistent than people thought. and the Fed's balance sheet has shrunk tremendously

insights.claim: Mallers dismisses the 2023 liquidity bounce as an artifact of the Silicon Valley Bank failure and Janet Yellen's reverse-repo engineering rather than a genuine easing cycle, making COVID-era 2021 the last true bull market.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: If the intervening liquidity was mechanical rather than structural, current positioning may be understating how starved the asset class has been.
insights.quote: we saw some liquidity injected into the system as a result of Silicon Valley Bank failing but that was this reverse repo Janet Yellen engineering

insights.claim: Mallers models Bitcoin as a hybrid of disruptive technology and future fiat-liquidity expectations — a tech asset that solved a new problem and disintermediates markets, but priced off expectations of money printing.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Resolves the 'trades like tech or like gold' debate into a two-factor model investors can decompose when attributing Bitcoin drawdowns.
insights.quote: Bitcoin is some combination of technology plus fiat liquidity

insights.claim: Mallers claims a 300 basis point Fed cut would send Bitcoin to $100,000 within a week, and notes Bitcoin weakened the same day on rumors the Fed might hike.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: A concrete rate-to-price sensitivity to trade against: Bitcoin is being priced as a pure liquidity beta at current levels, implying a spot price well below $100K.
insights.quote: If the Fed all of a sudden cuts 300 basis points, I think Bitcoin is going to hit 100K in a week.

insights.claim: Mallers expects new real all-time highs in the coming years driven by growth in expected fiat liquidity, money printing and credit, with technology adoption metrics like address counts and active balances following a slower, methodical path.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Sets a multi-year rather than multi-quarter horizon on the recovery thesis — relevant for sizing and for anyone underwriting near-term treasury-company solvency.
insights.quote: I I think that we'll reach new true real all-time highs um in the coming years because I expect the expectation of new fiat liquidity um and money printing and credit um to greatly grow

insights.claim: Mallers points to all-time-low consumer sentiment and a real K-shaped economy, with businesses now publicly urging the Fed to raise rates and fight inflation because their customers are too poor to shop.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: An unusual corporate-lobbying inversion — if firms are asking for tighter policy, the disinflation-plus-easing consensus for the next year may be mispriced.
insights.quote: you're seeing businesses now are very vocal with central planners and the Fed saying you have to raise rates and fight inflation because our customers are too poor to shop

insights.claim: Natalie Brunell says current sentiment toward Bitcoin treasury companies feels worse than the 2022 bear market and that she doubts the widely predicted $1 million Bitcoin by 2030 will materialize.
insights.speaker: Natalie Brunell, host
insights.so_what: Capitulation-grade sentiment from a long-time Bitcoin permabull host is itself a contrarian datapoint on positioning.
insights.quote: I've only been in a couple of these cycles, but it feels worse than even 2022.

insights.claim: Mallers argues bear markets are Bitcoin's self-governing mechanism for purging false promises and leverage-dependent operators who were only heroes while price rose, and warns that both bull and bear extremes exceed what participants expect.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Predicts more forced failures among levered Bitcoin-adjacent entities before the cycle turns — a reason to underweight leverage-dependent business models now.
insights.quote: however good you think a bull market can get, trust me, it will get better and however bad you think a bare market can get, trust me, it will get worse

insights.claim: Mallers notes he correctly anticipated rate hikes crushing Bitcoin's price in 2022 but did not anticipate Sam Bankman-Fried's roughly $10 billion fraud, illustrating that macro forecasting misses idiosyncratic blowups.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: A reminder to underwrite counterparty risk separately from macro risk when sizing crypto positions in a drawdown.
insights.quote: I knew rate hikes were going to come and Bitcoin's price was going to crash in 2022. I did not think Sam Bankman Freed had defrauded 10 billion dollars of the people's money

insights.claim: Strike is profitable and growing with fewer than 100 employees and holds over a hundred million dollars of Bitcoin on its balance sheet at roughly 50% off Bitcoin's highs, implying at least a quarter billion at new all-time highs.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Rare hard financials for a private Bitcoin company — headcount-light profitability plus a levered treasury is the profile he claims 21 could not achieve.
insights.quote: I mean, what we're 50% off highs and Strike has over $und00 million of Bitcoin on its balance sheet. So, assuming Bitcoin hits new all-time highs, we'll have at least a quart billion dollars with less than a hundred people working there.

insights.claim: Strike's Bitcoin per share rises every day because the business produces profit, giving it an accretion mechanism that does not depend on equity issuance or the mNAV premium.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: The structural argument for cash-flowing Bitcoin operators over pure treasury vehicles when capital markets close.
insights.quote: our Bitcoin per share goes up every day because we produce profit

insights.claim: Strike's product stack expanded demand-driven from clean Bitcoin buying into borrowing against Bitcoin and distributed multisig custody, then geographically from the US into Europe, the UK and Canada, which Mallers describes as having accidentally built a global Bitcoin bank.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Maps Strike's competitive surface: it now overlaps with Bitcoin-backed lenders and custody providers, not just exchanges.
insights.quote: what we've done just by being principled and being Bitcoiners and being simple is built this like global Bitcoin bank, Bitcoin financial institution

insights.claim: Mallers commits that Strike will not list altcoins and will not launch a prediction market, positioning against the two dominant revenue expansions among 2025-26 crypto platforms.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Deliberately forgone revenue lines — a differentiator versus Coinbase and Robinhood, but also a cap on Strike's addressable monetization.
insights.quote: I'm not going to list shitcoins on strike. I'm not going to launch prediction market.

insights.claim: Mallers argues a business's biggest competitor is its own cost base, because a company that spends more than it earns hands control of its future to outside capital — the lesson he draws from Mt. Gox, Coinbase, Binance and FTX each failing to become the Bitcoin company for the world.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: A screening rule for crypto operators: those dependent on continuous venture or capital-markets funding lose strategic control precisely in bear markets.
insights.quote: a business's biggest competitor are their costs because if you don't earn more than you spend, then the future of your business is not up to you anymore

insights.claim: Mallers says he intends to spend the majority of his newly freed time on Bitcoin content, podcasts and keynotes rather than founding new companies, having concluded that is where his marginal value lies.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Signals Strike's near-term growth strategy is top-of-funnel education rather than product proliferation or M&A.
insights.quote: I'm gonna spend majority of my new free time like doing more content doing doing these podcasts um going out creating keynotes. That is the feedback I've gotten on where my value now is.

insights.claim: Mallers says Strike is deliberately not decentralized in its decision-making — if a bug harms customers he can unilaterally credit every customer $20 — and contrasts that operating speed with the slow board-governed process at 21.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Operational velocity is Strike's claimed edge; the same trait is a key-man risk investors would have to price.
insights.quote: Bitcoin's very decentralized. Like, Strike's not. [laughter] If we need to do something and I decide we do it, we do it.

themes.theme: Adoption math and the self-custody debate

insights.claim: Mallers rejects the widely cited 1% global Bitcoin adoption figure — which would imply 80 million people out of 8 billion genuinely understand it — and estimates real understanding at closer to 800,000 people, roughly one basis point of humanity.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: If true adoption is 100x lower than consensus estimates, the runway argument for Bitcoin is far longer than most models assume.
insights.quote: I don't even think we're at 8 million. I I I would say we're closer to 800,000 and that's being generous.

insights.claim: Mallers argues ETF and 401k wrapper exposure does not count as adoption because a portfolio manager can flip the allocation off after an election, whereas someone who understands Bitcoin cannot be un-adopted.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Reframes ETF AUM as reversible flow rather than sticky ownership — a warning that institutional 'adoption' can reverse quickly on political change.
insights.quote: as soon as some money manager or some fund manager, some portfolio manager flips a switch the other way because someone else got elected president or whatever, then we're they're unadopted

insights.claim: Mallers says Bitcoin could become a $10-20 trillion asset — 10 to 20x from current levels, taking it from roughly half a million to $5 million per coin in his framing — while still remaining under 1% adoption, because global wealth is concentrated in a numerically small group that is now learning Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Decouples price upside from population adoption: the trade is about capturing wealth-weighted allocation, not headcount.
insights.quote: Bitcoin can become a 10 20 trillion asset which for everyone listening that's 10 to 20x from where it is today

insights.claim: Mallers argues price is the only KPI that matters for Bitcoin because it directly reflects marginal decisions by people choosing to store their labor in Bitcoin rather than dollars, treasuries or equity indices, dismissing 'in it for the technology' framing.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: A discipline for filtering Bitcoin narratives: on-chain and developer metrics are downstream of monetization, which price already aggregates.
insights.quote: people will say things like I'm not in it for the price. I'm in it for the technology. Get the

insights.claim: Mallers declines to treat self-custody as a religious test, saying what matters is that self-custody remains possible at any time because that optionality is what keeps custodial businesses and the network honest — and notes gold was demonetized precisely because it sat in concentrated vaults.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: The historical analogy to gold's vault concentration is the core structural risk to watch as ETF and custodial share of supply grows.
insights.quote: The reason gold was demonetized in the first place is it was all sitting in concentrated vault.

insights.claim: Mallers says he is not bothered by someone holding the BlackRock ETF if they understand money, and points out that Coinbase does not produce 'what is money' or Austrian theory content — leaving the education gap unaddressed by the largest incumbent.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Identifies where the adoption bottleneck actually sits — distribution exists, comprehension does not, which is where Strike is positioning its marketing spend.
insights.quote: Coinbase isn't making what is money videos, isn't making Austrian theory videos

insights.claim: Mallers reframes holding Bitcoin as a daily re-monetization decision rather than a multi-year bet, arguing investors should ask each morning whether Bitcoin or an alternative equity is the better store for value already created.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: A behavioral framework for holding through drawdowns that reframes opportunity cost as a recurring choice rather than sunk commitment.
insights.quote: don't mistaken this as like a I'm betting the next 5 years of my life. No, you're not. Every day, just wake up

insights.claim: Mallers refuses to apologize to investors who bought Bitcoin near 2021 highs and made a round trip, arguing there is no free lunch and that hindsight rotation between Bitcoin and Nvidia was never actually available.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Reflects that even core Bitcoin advocates are now openly conceding multi-year underperformance versus AI equities — a sentiment marker.
insights.quote: could you have invested in Nvidia instead of Bitcoin, but then Bitco if if you in hindsight could have went from Bitcoin, but then Nvidia for this time, but then back to Bitcoin and then you're right.

themes.theme: Bitcoin as an uncorruptible truth mechanism

insights.claim: Mallers' central thesis is that Bitcoin can change the world because the world cannot change Bitcoin, and that this non-negotiability — refusing to bend for Wall Street, corporations or governments — is the source of its appeal and the standard he applied to his own decision to leave 21.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: The ideological constraint that will govern Strike's future decisions — useful for predicting what deals Strike will and won't do.
insights.quote: Bitcoin can change the world because the world can't change Bitcoin

insights.claim: Mallers separates domains where human intervention is legitimate (lawns, wedding florals) from domains where it destroys the signal (a doctor smoothing over blood work, money), placing money firmly in the second category because truth is what allows response and improvement.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: A clean rhetorical framework for the hard-money case that separates anti-intervention ideology from a narrower claim about monetary information.
insights.quote: there are some things in life that we cannot intervene with the teacher, with truth

insights.claim: Mallers describes money as human dignity and argues that printing the currency people work for is an affront to that dignity — the emotional core of what he says converts people, not price charts.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Identifies the actual conversion mechanism for retail adoption, which is narrative and grievance-driven rather than return-driven.
insights.quote: money is human dignity

insights.claim: Mallers frames self-custodied Bitcoin as uniquely immune to both debasement and local taxation — twelve words in his head that Chicago cannot raise property taxes on — as the basis for preferring it over gold or real estate.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Articulates the seizure- and tax-resistance premium that he believes remains unpriced relative to physical stores of value.
insights.quote: It's not like Chicago can increase the property taxes on my Bitcoin. It's 12 words in my head.

insights.claim: Mallers says the Bitcoin community's implicit demand of him — repeated by strangers who approached him during the 21 crisis — was 'don't sell out, don't give up control,' which he treats as evidence that a credible non-compromised Bitcoin company is itself a scarce asset.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: Brand trust is Strike's real moat versus better-capitalized competitors; erosion of it would be the leading indicator of trouble.
insights.quote: please don't like whatever you do we trust you just don't sell out don't give up control

insights.claim: Mallers argues failure should be owned rather than deflected, describing a Strike culture rule that punishes finger-pointing because blaming others concedes that someone else controls your outcomes.
insights.speaker: Jack Mallers
insights.so_what: A management-culture datapoint for assessing Strike's internal durability under stress.
insights.quote: I don't believe in pointing fingers because then that by proxy assumes that you're not in control of your own life
